statement: If a straight line touch a circle, and a straight line be joined from the centre to the point of contact, the straight line so joined will be perpendicular to the tangent.
heath_proof: For let a straight line DE touch the circle ABC at the point C, let the centre F of the circle ABC be taken, and let FC be joined from F to C; I say that FC is perpendicular to DE. For, if not, let FG be drawn from F perpendicular to DE. Then, since the angle FGC is right, the angle FCG is acute; [I. 17]and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side; [I. 19] therefore FC is greater than FG. But FC is equal to FB; therefore FB is also greater than FG, the less than the greater: which is impossible. Therefore FG is not perpendicular to DE. Similarly we can prove that neither is any other straight line except FC; therefore FC is perpendicular to DE.
ai_proof_text:
3.18
**Statement:** If a straight line touch a circle, and a straight line be joined from the centre to the point of contact, the straight line so joined will be perpendicular to the tangent.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line DE touch the circle ABC at the point C, let the centre F of the circle ABC be taken (3.1), and let FC be joined from F to C (P1). I say that FC is perpendicular to DE.

**Step 2.** Suppose that FC is not perpendicular to DE. The centre F lies within the circle, and DE, since it touches the circle, does not cut it (D3.2); hence F is not on DE. From F draw FG perpendicular to DE, DE being regarded as produced as far as necessary (1.12), and let G be the foot of this perpendicular on DE. The point G is not the point C: for if G coincided with C, the perpendicular FG would be the very line FC, and FC would be perpendicular to DE, contrary to the supposition.

**Step 3.** Since FG is perpendicular to DE, the angle FGC is right (D1.10). In the triangle FGC the two angles FGC and FCG together are less than two right angles (1.17); since the angle FGC is itself a right angle, the angle FCG is less than a right angle. Therefore the angle FGC is greater than the angle FCG.

**Step 4.** In any triangle the greater angle is subtended by the greater side (1.19). In the triangle FGC the side FC subtends the greater angle FGC and the side FG subtends the lesser angle FCG; therefore FC is greater than FG.

**Step 5.** Since DE touches the circle ABC, it meets the circle and, being produced, does not cut the circle (D3.2). Moreover DE meets the circle at no point other than C: for if it met the circle at a second point H, the straight line CH joining two points of the circumference would fall within the circle (3.2), so that DE would cut the circle, contrary to D3.2. Hence G, being a point of DE different from C, lies neither on the circumference nor within the circle; that is, G lies outside the circle.

**Step 6.** The centre F lies within the circle and G lies outside it; therefore the straight line FG passes across the circumference. Let FG meet the circumference at the point B. Then FB is a part of FG, so that FG is greater than FB (CN5).

**Step 7.** Since F is the centre and B, C are points on the circumference, FB is equal to FC (D1.15). By Step 4, FC is greater than FG; hence FB, being equal to FC, is also greater than FG. But by Step 6, FG is greater than FB. Thus FB would be at once greater than and less than FG, which is impossible.

**Step 8.** Therefore the supposition of Step 2 is false, and FC is perpendicular to DE. Hence, if a straight line touch a circle, and a straight line be joined from the centre to the point of contact, the straight line so joined is perpendicular to the tangent. Q.E.D.
